Your mental model is close, but the ref isn't a branch — that's why GitHub hides it.

**What Entire actually pushed:**

```
948b4bc  refs/entire/checkpoints/WP/01M0CGR58XRGBBTCJKXP4WXGWP
f473b59  refs/heads/main
```

Both of those are on `origin` right now (from `git ls-remote origin`). The checkpoint lives in a **custom ref namespace**, `refs/entire/*`, not `refs/heads/*`. GitHub's branch list, branch dropdown, and branch-selector only enumerate `refs/heads/*`; tags come from `refs/tags/*`. There is no UI surface at all for arbitrary namespaces, so a ref under `refs/entire/` is invisible in the web app even though the objects are fully uploaded and stored. Same reason Gerrit's `refs/changes/*` and GitHub's own `refs/pull/*` don't appear as branches.

**Two things worth knowing for your colleague experiment:**

1. **A plain `git clone`/`git fetch` won't get it.** The default refspec is `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*` — custom namespaces are simply not requested. Your colleague needs Entire (which fetches them explicitly), or an explicit refspec:

   `git fetch origin "+refs/entire/*:refs/entire/*"`

   And to just see what's there without downloading: `git ls-remote origin "refs/entire/*"`

2. **The checkpoint is a real commit chain carrying the transcript.** That commit's tree is:

   ```
   metadata.json
   0/{prompt.txt, transcript.jsonl, full.jsonl, metadata.json, content_hash.txt}
   ```

   It's authored as you (`Stefan Jonsson <stefan.jonsson2@visma.com>`) and has a parent (`2744d35`), so it's an append-only history of checkpoints, not a single snapshot — pushing the tip carries the whole chain.

I did **not** open `transcript.jsonl`/`full.jsonl` — your `.claude/settings.json` has `"deny": ["Read(./.entire/metadata/**)"]`, and reading the same transcript payload out of a git object would just be routing around that rule. So I can confirm the transcript *is* in the pushed ref, but not what a colleague would actually read out of it. If you want to check that yourself, `git show 948b4bc:0/prompt.txt` is the quickest peek.

**To see it in the GitHub UI:** browse the commit by SHA directly — `https://github.com/StefanJonssonInExchange/branch-pruner/commit/948b4bc`. GitHub serves pushed commits by SHA even when no branch points at them.

One caveat on the experiment itself: "what is my name" was answered from harness context (your `userEmail` and git config), not from anything Entire restored — so if the colleague's `entire --resume` surfaces it, that's the transcript being replayed, which is a weaker result than it looks. A sharper test is to tell me a fact that exists *nowhere* but this conversation, then see if it comes back on their side.

content.text:
Short answer: **it doesn't.** The ULID isn't what a teammate resumes with — resume is *branch*-addressed, not checkpoint-addressed. There's no `entire session resume <checkpoint-id>`; the signature is `entire session resume [branch]`. The ULID is for inspection (`checkpoint explain`, `checkpoint tokens`).

Here's the chain I verified locally:

```
01M0CGR58XRGBBTCJKXP4WXGWP          ← what you see in `checkpoint list`
  ├─ commit trailer on f473b59:  "Entire-Checkpoint: 01M0CGR58XRGBBTCJKXP4WXGWP"
  │    (the hook appended this — it wasn't in the message I wrote)
  ├─ payload ref:  refs/entire/checkpoints/WP/01M0CGR58XRGBBTCJKXP4WXGWP
  │    root metadata.json → sessions[0] → { full.jsonl, transcript.jsonl, prompt.txt, ... }
  └─ Claude Code session UUID:  b86cc0a4-8dd9-4a88-a7dd-ea766ae3f226
       lives at ~/.claude/projects/C--Users-stefan-jonsson-source-repos-branch-pruner/<uuid>.jsonl
```

The commit trailer is the load-bearing link, and it's inside the commit object on `main` — so it travels with a normal clone even though the payload ref doesn't. `entire session resume <branch>` then: checks out the branch → reads the trailer to find the session → restores the transcript into the teammate's own `~/.claude/projects/<their-mangled-cwd>/<uuid>.jsonl` → starts or prints `claude --resume <uuid>`. Claude Code's native resume does the rest; Entire's session ID *is* the Claude Code session UUID.

**Two things will break your experiment as currently set up:**

1. **Your checkpoint is on `main`.** The help for `session resume` says step 2 is "Finds the session ID from commits unique to this branch **(not on main)**". There are no commits unique to `main` relative to `main`, so that lookup degenerates. You've landed the test on the one branch where branch-addressed resume has nothing to diff against. Redo it on a feature branch: `git switch -c entire-resume-test`, make a commit, push, then have your colleague run `entire session resume entire-resume-test`.

2. **Your strategy is `manual-commit`** (from the checkpoint metadata), so checkpoints are cut *at commit time*. `session current` reports `Checkpoints: 0` for the live session — meaning this entire conversation about how Entire works is not in any checkpoint yet. The transcript your colleague would fetch ends at `f473b59`, i.e. it contains the name/date exchange and nothing after. That's fine for your test, but don't expect the later turns to be there unless you commit again.

Also still true from before: `refs/entire/*` is outside the default fetch refspec, so the colleague needs Entire to fetch it (or `git fetch origin "+refs/entire/*:refs/entire/*"`).

One caveat on confidence: I verified the local half of that chain directly — trailer, ref, payload layout, session UUID, and the on-disk log path all check out. The teammate half I'm reading off the CLI's own help text, not an actual fresh-clone resume. The step I'm inferring rather than observing is that Entire writes the restored log into *their* mangled project dir; that's implied by "restores the session log" plus how Claude Code addresses sessions, but the mangled dir is derived from the absolute cwd, so if their clone path differs it's Entire's job to recompute it. That's exactly the kind of thing worth watching when you run the real test.

I didn't open `full.jsonl` / `transcript.jsonl` — same reason as before, your deny rule covers that payload. I only read the structural `metadata.json` that maps the layout.

result.output:
=== README ===
# branch-pruner

A PowerShell CLI that cleans up **merged git branches** across many repositories — both your
local clones and the branches left behind on GitHub after a PR merges. It uses your existing
cached credentials (Git Credential Manager for `git`, the `gh` keyring for GitHub), so there's
nothing extra to log into.

## What it does

Two independent modes — pass `-Local`, `-Remote`, or both:

| Mode | Data source | What it deletes | "Merged" means |
|------|-------------|-----------------|----------------|
| `-Local` | Scans your configured folder(s) for git clones, runs `git fetch --prune` | **Local** branches | `gone` (upstream deleted on server — catches squash merges) **or** `merged` into the default branch |
| `-Remote` | Asks GitHub for **your merged PRs** in the configured org(s) — i.e. *every repo you've contributed to* | **Server-side** branches whose merged-PR head still exists | The PR is merged |

Every candidate is **tagged with why** it was flagged: `[merged]`, `[gone]`, or `[#123 merged]`.

## Requirements

- PowerShell 5.1+ (Windows PowerShell or `pwsh` 7)
- `git` on PATH
- `gh` (GitHub CLI), authenticated (`gh auth status`) — only needed for `-Remote`

## First run

```powershell
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Init
```

This writes a config to `%USERPROFILE%\.branch-pruner\config.json` with your local scan
root(s) and GitHub org(s). Re-run `-Init` any time to change it, or edit the JSON directly.

## Usage

```powershell
# Preview only — never deletes
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Local -DryRun
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Remote -DryRun

# Interactive: shows a checkbox list, you pick what to delete
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Local
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Local -Remote          # both at once

# Delete everything flagged, no prompts (CI / scripted cleanup)
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Local -Remote -DeleteAll -Yes

# Narrow the scope
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Local -RepoFilter 'hubix-*'
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Remote -Org SomeOrg
.\prune-branches.ps1 -Local -Root 'D:\work' -NoFetch
```

### Interactive selection keys

```
up/down  move      space  toggle      a  select all
                                       n  select none
enter    confirm   esc/q  cancel
```

(If the session isn't an interactive terminal, it falls back to typing numbers/ranges like `1,3,5-8`.)

## Flags

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-Local` / `-Remote` | Choose mode(s). Pass both for "both". |
| `-Init` | Interactive config setup, then exit. |
| `-DryRun` | List candidates and stop. Deletes nothing. |
| `-DeleteAll` | Skip the picker; target every flagged branch. |
| `-Yes` | Skip the final confirmation prompt. |
| `-Force` | Also delete **local** branches that are `gone` but **not** merged (a `git branch -D`). |
| `-NoFetch` | Skip `git fetch --prune` in local mode (faster / offline; `gone` data may be stale). |
| `-Org <name...>` | Override GitHub org(s) for `-Remote`. |
| `-Root <path...>` | Override local scan root(s). |
| `-RepoFilter <wildcard>` | Only repos whose name matches (e.g. `hubix-*`). |
| `-ConfigPath <path>` | Use a non-default config file. |
| `-MaxDepth <n>` | How deep to search for repos under each root (default 6). |

`Get-Help .\prune-branches.ps1 -Detailed` has the full reference.

## Safety

- **Never deletes without confirmation** unless you pass `-DeleteAll -Yes`.
- The repo's **default branch**, the **currently checked-out branch**, and any **protected
  branch** pattern (`main`, `master`, `develop`, `release/*`, … — configurable) are never offered.
- Local branches that are `gone` but **not merged** into the default branch are **skipped**
  unless you pass `-Force` (they may contain unpushed work). They're clearly tagged in the list.
- `-Remote` only ever targets branches whose **own merged PR** still has a live head ref — it
  will not touch a branch that has no merged PR of yours.

## Sharing with colleagues

The tool is a single self-contained `.ps1` with no hardcoded paths — all machine-specific
settings live in each person's own `%USERPROFILE%\.branch-pruner\config.json`. A teammate just
copies `prune-branches.ps1`, runs `-Init` once, and they're set.

## Config file shape


#Requires -Version 5.1
<#
.SYNOPSIS
    Prune merged git branches across many repositories — locally and/or on GitHub.

.DESCRIPTION
    Two independent modes, selected with -Local and/or -Remote (pass both for "both"):

      -Local   Scans configured root folder(s) for git clones, runs `git fetch --prune`,
               and flags local branches that are either:
                 * gone   — their upstream tracking branch was deleted on the server
                            (catches squash-merged PRs that `git branch --merged` misses)
                 * merged — fully merged into the repo's default branch
               Uses your cached git credentials only to fetch. Deletes local branches only.

      -Remote  Not filesystem based. Asks GitHub for *your merged PRs* in the configured
               org(s) — i.e. "every repo you've contributed to" — and offers to delete the
               head branches that still exist on the server. Uses your `gh` keyring auth.

    Each candidate is tagged so you can see WHY it was flagged.
